Mixture-of-experts (MoE) transformers route each token to a small subset of specialized feed-forward "expert" modules via a learned gating network, achieving high parameter counts without proportionally higher compute — but this economy depends entirely on the router distributing tokens roughly evenly across experts. The central question is: when you fine-tune a pretrained MoE on a narrow downstream distribution, does the router's learned routing policy degrade in ways that are hard to detect but catastrophically harm generalization or efficiency? The key concepts are the auxiliary load-balancing loss (typically added during pretraining to penalize routing collapse, where one expert monopolizes traffic), the distinction between expert utilization and expert specialization (a router can appear balanced by utilization metrics while actually routing semantically identical tokens to different experts, destroying specialization), and the interaction between the gating temperature and gradient dynamics during fine-tuning. A beginner worries about accuracy on the fine-tuning benchmark; an expert worries that the auxiliary loss weight tuned for pretraining data statistics is now miscalibrated for the fine-tuning distribution, that experts which were dormant on the pretraining domain silently receive zero gradient and become dead weights, and that the router can "collapse" not in a single dramatic failure but through gradual drift — appearing healthy on load metrics while the specialization structure that made the model efficient quietly disintegrates. The failure mode that really bites is that standard evaluation catches none of this: held-out loss looks fine, but inference efficiency degrades and the model has effectively become a dense network with expensive routing overhead.

The auxiliary loss enforces a frequency constraint — it penalizes unequal token counts per expert — but says nothing about which tokens go where, so the router can satisfy the loss perfectly while scrambling the semantic assignment of tokens to experts across fine-tuning steps. Concretely, imagine expert 7 learned during pretraining to handle syntactic dependency heads and expert 12 handled named entities; after fine-tuning on a narrow domain (say, medical QA), the router may reassign named-entity tokens to expert 7 and dependency heads to expert 12 simply because the gradient signal from the new distribution makes that a lower-loss configuration — utilization stays flat, but the internal "contract" between token type and expert is inverted. This is sometimes called routing churn, and Zoph et al.'s Switch Transformer work (2022) noted that routing decisions are surprisingly unstable even with load balancing active, with significant fractions of tokens changing their expert assignment across checkpoints without corresponding loss spikes. The detection problem without pretraining data is genuinely hard, but tractable approaches include: (1) computing the Jensen-Shannon divergence between the router's per-expert input distributions across fine-tuning checkpoints — collapsing specialization shows as distributions converging toward each other even as marginal utilization stays uniform; (2) probing expert activations with a lightweight classifier trained to predict token syntactic/semantic category from a single expert's hidden state, where degrading specialization shows as inter-expert classifier accuracy equalizing; and (3) tracking the routing agreement rate on a small frozen reference set drawn from the fine-tuning data itself across checkpoints, flagging instability when agreement drops below ~70%, a threshold used informally in some internal Google Brain analyses. The key insight an expert holds that a beginner misses is that the auxiliary loss was never designed to preserve specialization — it was designed to prevent hardware underutilization — so using it as a proxy for specialization health is a category error.

When fine-tuning on a low-diversity corpus, the router's softmax outputs sharpen — the winning expert's logit dominates more consistently because the input distribution is narrow and predictable — which means the gradient of the gating loss with respect to the router weights flows almost entirely through the top-1 or top-2 selected experts and nearly zero through the rest. This is a form of the straight-through estimator problem made worse by corpus narrowness: the non-selected experts receive no direct gradient from the task loss (they aren't computed), and the auxiliary load-balancing gradient, which is the only signal reaching them, is small relative to the task gradient when fine-tuning learning rates are set aggressively. Standard fine-tuning practice makes this significantly worse on two counts: practitioners typically use the same learning rate for all parameters including the router, and they rarely re-tune the auxiliary loss coefficient λ, which was calibrated for pretraining data entropy — on a low-diversity corpus the effective token distribution entropy can drop by 30–50%, meaning λ needs to increase substantially just to maintain the same regularization pressure, but nobody does this. The Mixtral and GLaM training reports both note that λ is highly sensitive to data diversity and requires schedule adjustment, yet virtually every fine-tuning recipe treats it as a frozen hyperparameter. The practical outcome is a positive feedback loop: sharp routing → sparse gradients → router weights update only for the dominant path → routing gets sharper → previously marginally-used experts fall below the selection threshold entirely and receive zero gradient for the remainder of fine-tuning, becoming permanently dead. Mistral's internal ablations (reported informally at a 2023 workshop) suggested that as few as 10k fine-tuning steps on a narrow domain corpus could produce expert death rates above 15% in top-2 routing with standard λ settings.

There is essentially no theoretical justification for treating them identically — it's an operational convenience that was inherited from dense transformer training and never seriously challenged in early MoE work. The router is a small linear projection (in Switch Transformer, literally a single weight matrix of shape d_model × n_experts) whose job is to make a discrete, approximately correct selection decision, while each expert is a full FFN whose job is to learn a smooth function over its assigned token subspace; these have different loss landscape geometries, different gradient variance profiles, and different optimal update magnitudes. Adam's adaptive learning rate partially masks this problem because the router's gradient moments are estimated separately, but Adam was not designed to handle the non-stationarity introduced by discrete routing — when the routing assignment changes, the expert's optimizer state (accumulated first and second moment estimates) becomes stale relative to its new token distribution, yet the moments persist and actively bias subsequent updates in the wrong direction. Lewis et al.'s BASE Layers paper (2021) and the later Expert Choice routing paper (Zhou et al., 2022) both implicitly acknowledge this by experimenting with frozen or slowly-updated routers, finding that decoupling router update frequency from expert update frequency improved stability — Expert Choice's design of letting experts select tokens rather than tokens selecting experts is partly motivated by wanting smoother gradient flow properties. The cleanest theoretical framing comes from viewing the router as a latent variable model parameter and the experts as likelihood parameters — in EM terms, the router is the E-step and the experts are the M-step, and these canonically require different update schedules and should not share momentum state. In practice, a simple intervention — using a lower learning rate multiplier (0.1–0.3×) on router weights, or resetting router optimizer state at the start of fine-tuning while keeping expert states — is almost never done but would likely reduce routing churn substantially based on the gradient variance arguments alone.

The failure mode is that the router converges to a locally consistent but globally suboptimal assignment — it finds the best mapping from new-domain tokens to the existing expert basis, but if that basis doesn't span the functions needed for the new domain, the router's "solution" is a least-bad compromise that looks stable by all routing metrics while the model's task performance plateaus well below what the parameter count should allow. Concretely, if you fine-tune a pretrained MoE on code generation after pretraining on natural language, the existing experts may have no unit that specializes in, say, type-system reasoning or scope resolution — the router will route those tokens to the closest available expert (perhaps one that handled logical connectives in natural language), the expert will receive gradient and drift toward the new function, but it will do so while still being routed tokens from its original domain in any mixed-distribution evaluation, creating a destructive interference pattern where one expert is being pulled in two incompatible directions simultaneously. Detection without access to pretraining data is possible through expert saturation probing: for each expert, fit a low-rank linear probe predicting the residual error of that expert's output on fine-tuning data — if the probe explains substantial variance (say R² > 0.3), the expert's current representations are systematically missing structure that a linear correction could provide, indicating the basis is inadequate for the domain. A complementary signal is the inter-expert output similarity measured via centered kernel alignment (CKA) across fine-tuning: if experts that were functionally distinct at pretraining (low CKA) converge toward higher CKA on fine-tuning data, it indicates the domain is forcing multiple experts into the same functional role because none of them are adequate alone — Nguyen et al.'s CKA analysis of dense transformers (2021) showed this convergence pattern correlates with representational bottlenecks, and the same diagnostic transfers directly to MoE experts. The practical intervention implied by detection is to selectively unfreeze and reinitialize experts whose saturation probe R² exceeds threshold before router training begins — essentially a domain-adaptive basis augmentation — but this requires deciding how many experts to sacrifice from the pretrained basis, which is a direct tradeoff against the model's ability to handle mixed-domain inference after fine-tuning.

One specific, non-obvious fact: the load-balancing auxiliary loss, when applied during fine-tuning, can actively cause the specialization collapse it was designed to prevent, through a mechanism involving the interaction between the loss gradient and the fine-tuning data's token frequency distribution. Here's the precise mechanism: the auxiliary loss penalizes deviation from uniform expert utilization, so if the fine-tuning corpus has a skewed token type distribution (which narrow-domain corpora almost always do — medical text has far more noun phrases than imperatives, code has far more identifiers than conjunctions), the auxiliary loss gradient will push the router to compensate by routing some high-frequency token types away from their natural expert toward underutilized experts, not because those experts are functionally appropriate but purely to satisfy the uniformity constraint. The non-obvious implication is that the correct λ during fine-tuning is not a scaled-down version of the pretraining λ but potentially zero or even negative (a load-imbalance encouragement), because on a narrow domain you may actually want the router to collapse onto the 2-3 experts that genuinely span the domain's functional requirements and stop wasting compute routing tokens to irrelevant experts that will never develop useful specialization for this domain. This inverts the standard intuition entirely: for narrow fine-tuning, controlled routing collapse onto a domain-relevant expert subset may be the optimal strategy, and fighting it with auxiliary losses is fighting the data.
